extracted.intended_audience: Applicants seeking Royal Society endorsement for the UK Global Talent (formerly Tier 1 Exceptional Talent/Promise) visa; immigration forum participants
extracted.subtask_description: Practical peer-discussion guidance about applying to the Royal Society for endorsement under the UK Global Talent visa (Exceptional Promise/Talent), including what evidence is expected, common refusal wording, and appeal timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant’s track record relative to career stage
rubrics_metrics.description: “applicant’s track record and contributions to the field to date, relative to career stage” — the central reason cited for refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors compare an applicant’s achievements against expectations for their career stage/age: the same achievement may be 'exceptional' for a younger researcher but insufficient for a more senior applicant. Applicants who started late, changed careers, or had interruptions may be disadvantaged in practice even though guidelines state gaps shouldn't affect outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category: Exceptional Promise vs Exceptional Talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the applicant applied under Exceptional Promise or Exceptional Talent matters for expectations and evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptional Promise targets early-career researchers; expectations are scaled to career stage. Applicants should choose the category matching their career level and provide evidence appropriate to that category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic qualifications and research publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of a PhD and published research articles are commonly cited evidence of merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a PhD and publications are important supporting evidence, forum members report that having them does not guarantee endorsement — the overall track record relative to career stage is still decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference letter from someone in the UK
rubrics_metrics.description: A letter from a UK-based person is required/expected (explicitly listed for the Promise category).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the Promise category, applicants need a letter from a UK person; this is among the key documents reviewers look for. The quality and standing of the referee may influence the assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required documentation for Promise category
rubrics_metrics.description: For the Promise category applicants need: letter from UK person, personal statement, CV and application form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all documents listed in the Royal Society guidelines are submitted. Missing or weak documentation can reduce chances of endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional society or body membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership of a relevant professional engineering/science body (UK or elsewhere) may strengthen an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forum discussion asks whether applicants are members of professional bodies, implying evaluators may consider such affiliations as evidence of standing; absence of membership does not preclude endorsement but may be a weaker profile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current employment context (industry vs university research)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an applicant is working in industry R&D or academic research may be factored into assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors ask about current sector, suggesting reviewers consider the applicant’s role and the relevance/impact of their work within their employment context when judging contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjectivity of 'exceptional' and comparative evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'exceptional' is subjective; panels evaluate exceptionality comparatively across applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should present clear, comparative evidence of exceptional contributions (e.g., high-impact outputs, leadership, awards). Expect variability in panel judgements; what is exceptional for one career stage may not be for another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback form and level of detail on refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal communications may include a standard endorsement form PDF and a separate PDF with detailed feedback, but often the feedback is a short, ambiguous phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forum reports indicate refusals commonly give the same brief reason without detailed critique. Applicants seeking to appeal should request detailed feedback, but it may not always be forthcoming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal / review process and timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants can request a review of the decision; reported response times in the forum include about 26 working days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If planning to appeal, allow weeks for the review outcome and retain copies of the original refusal PDFs. Preparing targeted additional evidence addressing the stated reason (track record relative to career stage) may help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity of Royal Society applications and rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Forum members note comparatively few apply to the Royal Society and rejections may therefore be less common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is observational (peer forum perception) rather than an official criterion, but applicants should be aware that panels may have high standards and low application volumes do not guarantee endorsement.
